section: 12.1 Concord: The General Rule

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
What is concord in English grammar?

The term **concord** refers to the **agreement between the Subject and the Verb in Person and Number**.

The general rule is: a **singular subject** takes a **singular verb**, and a **plural subject** takes a **plural verb**.

section: 12.1 Concord: The General Rule

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
Can you show the general rule of concord with examples?

| A — singular subject + singular verb | B — plural subject + plural verb |
|---|---|
| A cow **gives** milk. | Cows **give** milk. |
| A lion **roars**. | Lions **roar**. |
| He **likes** music. | They **like** music. |
| She **sings** well. | They **sing** well. |
| This book **is** good. | These books **are** good. |
| That mango **is** bad. | Those mangoes **are** bad. |

All the sentences in Group A have **singular subjects and singular verbs**; all those in Group B have **plural subjects and plural verbs**.

Note that in the present tense a singular (third-person) verb usually ends in **-s/-es** (*gives, roars*), while a plural noun usually ends in -s (*cows, lions*) and its verb does not.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Subjects Joined by 'and' (Rules 1-3)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
What verb do we use when two subjects are joined by 'and'?

**Rule 1:** When two or more nouns or pronouns are combined by **and** to form a **compound subject**, the verb must be **plural**:
- Gopal and Ganesh **are** cousins.
- Balu, Suresh and David **have** come.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Subjects Joined by 'and' (Rules 1-3)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
How does repeating the article or possessive before two nouns joined by 'and' affect the verb?

**Rule 2:** When the **article** or **possessive pronoun** is **repeated** before two nouns connected by *and*, two different persons are meant, so the verb is **plural**. When it is used **only once**, one person with two roles is meant, so the verb is **singular**:

| Two persons (plural verb) | One person (singular verb) |
|---|---|
| A poet and **a** critic **are** visiting our college. | A poet and critic **is** visiting our college. |
| My uncle and **my** guardian **are** helping me. | My uncle and guardian **is** helping me. |
| The secretary and **the** cashier **were** arrested. | The secretary and cashier **was** arrested. |

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Subjects Joined by 'and' (Rules 1-3)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
When do two nouns joined by 'and' take a singular verb?

**Rule 3:** When two nouns connected by *and* **stand for one idea** (a single thing or notion), the verb must be **singular**:
- Bread and butter **was** served for breakfast. (one dish)
- Time and tide **waits** for no man.
- All work and no play **is** not a good habit.
- Pen and ink **is** what I want now.
- The sum and substance of the matter **is** known to everybody.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: 'as well as', 'with', etc. (Rule 4)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
What verb do we use when two nouns are connected by 'as well as', 'with' or 'together with'?

**Rule 4:** When two nouns are connected by **as well as, with, along with, together with, in addition to, accompanied by, as much as, rather than, in the company of, more than**, etc., the verb must agree with the **first noun** (the real subject). The second noun is only an addition and does not change the number:
- The President as well as the members **was** present.
- The President, with all his staff, **is** attending the function.
- Sita, more than her classmates, **is** liked by everyone.
- The robber, together with his gang, **was** captured.
- The students, rather than the bus conductor, **were** responsible for the trouble.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Collective Nouns (Rule 5)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
Do collective nouns take a singular or a plural verb?

**Rule 5:** Collective nouns representing groups may be used as:
- **singular** when the group is taken **as a unit**, and
- **plural** when the **individual members** are taken into consideration.

Examples:
- Our team **is** playing today. (the team as one unit)
- The team **are** taking rest now. (the individual players)
- The clergy **is** not to blame. / The clergy **are** against the new law.
- The Government **welcomes** the proposal. (one body acting as a unit)
- The Government **are** discussing the proposal. (the members discussing among themselves)

Words like **class, assembly, audience, family, staff, committee, council, crew, commission**, etc. belong to this type.

**Usage note:** The plural use (*The team are...*) is common in British and Indian English. American English usually treats such nouns as singular (*The team is...*) and may say *The team members are...* instead.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Collective Nouns (Rule 5)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
Are 'police' and 'cattle' singular or plural?

**Police** and **cattle** are **always plural**, even though they don't end in -s:
- The cattle **are** in the field.
- The police **are** vigilant.

(To speak of one, say *a police officer*, *a cow / an animal*.)

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Collective Nouns (Rule 5)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
Is 'public' singular or plural?

**Public** can be used **both as singular and as plural**:
- The public **is** / **are** not allowed to enter the court rooms.

The singular treats the public as one body; the plural thinks of the individual people.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Plural Form, Singular Meaning (Rules 6-7)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
What verb follows nouns like 'news', 'measles' and 'politics'?

**Rule 6:** Some nouns are **plural in form but singular in meaning**. They are followed by **singular verbs**:
- The news of her husband's death **has** shattered her.
- Measles **is** a common disease.
- Politics **is** not everyone's game.
- The United States **is** the only superpower now. (one country)
- *The Three Musketeers* **is** an interesting book. (the title of one book)

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Plural Form, Singular Meaning (Rules 6-7)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
Do plural amounts like 'six feet' or 'ten rupees' take a plural verb?

**Rule 7:** When a plural number applies to **heights, weights, distances or amounts of money**, the whole amount is treated as **one quantity**, so it takes a **singular verb**:
- Six feet **is** a good height.
- Fifty kilograms **is** not a small weight.
- Twenty-five kilometres **is** certainly a great distance to walk.
- Ten rupees **is** just enough for the bus fare.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Introductory 'there' (Rule 8)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
Does 'there is' or 'there are' depend on the word 'there'?

**Rule 8:** The introductory **there** is not the real subject. It takes a singular or plural verb depending on the number of the **real subject**, which comes after the verb:
- There **is** a beggar at the gate. (real subject: *a beggar* — singular)
- There **are** some famous pictures in the art gallery. (real subject: *some famous pictures* — plural)

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: one of, a lot of, many a, a good many (Rules 9-13)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
Does 'one of the players' take a singular or a plural verb?

**Rule 9:** The subject **one of** followed by a plural noun takes a **singular verb**, to agree with **one** (the real subject):
- One of the players **was** injured during the match.
- One of my friends **has** been selected to the university cricket team.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: one of, a lot of, many a, a good many (Rules 9-13)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
Do 'a lot of', 'plenty of', 'most of' and 'some of' take a singular or plural verb?

**Rule 10:** **A lot of, plenty of, most of, some of** (and similar expressions) take:
- a **singular** verb when followed by an **uncountable noun**, and
- a **plural** verb when followed by a **countable (plural) noun**.

Uncountable — singular verb:
- A lot of water **has** overflowed the tank.
- Plenty of milk **is** available.
- Most of the money **has** been spent.
- A great deal of information **has** been collected from the secretary.

Countable — plural verb:
- A lot of people **were** present at the funeral.
- Some of those who attended the function **were** from far-off places.

**Note:** *A great deal of* is normally used only with **uncountable** nouns (*a great deal of information / discussion*). With plural countable nouns, standard English uses **a great many**: *A great many discussions **have** taken place on the matter.*

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: one of, a lot of, many a, a good many (Rules 9-13)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
Which nouns have the same form in the singular and plural, and what verb do they take?

**Rule 11:** Nouns like **series, species, means, gallows, headquarters, innings, deer, sheep, aircraft**, etc. have the **same form for both singular and plural**. The verb can be either **singular or plural**, depending on the meaning:
- A sheep **was** run over by a car. (one sheep)
- Sheep **are** meek animals. (sheep in general — plural)
- An aircraft **was** damaged while taking off. (one)
- Several aircraft **were** damaged during the war. (more than one)

Look at the determiner (*a, an, several, these*) to decide the number.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: one of, a lot of, many a, a good many (Rules 9-13)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
What verb follows 'many a' and 'more than one'?

**Rule 12:** **Many a** and **more than one** take a **singular noun** and a **singular verb** (even though the meaning is plural):
- Many a passenger **was** hurt in the accident.
- More than one attempt **has** been made to break the lock.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: one of, a lot of, many a, a good many (Rules 9-13)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
What verb follows 'a good many'?

**Rule 13:** **A good many** is followed by a **plural noun** and a **plural verb**:
- A good many passengers **were** stranded on their way.

Compare: *Many a passenger **was**...* (singular noun, singular verb) vs. *A good many passengers **were**...* (plural noun, plural verb).

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Nouns Involving Pairs (Rule 14)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
What verb do we use with 'scissors', 'trousers' and 'spectacles'?

**Rule 14:** Nouns involving **pairs**, like **scissors, trousers, pants, tongs, shoes, knickers, spectacles, pliers, binoculars**, etc., are **plural**, and the verb should also be **plural**:
- Those spectacles **are** of no use to me.
- Those scissors **were** very blunt.

If **a pair of** is used before them, the verb is then **singular** (it agrees with *pair*):
- A pair of shoes **is** very expensive nowadays.

What is the difference between "A poet and a critic are visiting our college" and "A poet and critic is visiting our college"?

With the article **repeated** (*a poet and **a** critic*), two different persons are meant, so the verb is plural: **are**.
With the article used **once** (*a poet and critic*), one person who is both a poet and a critic is meant, so the verb is singular: **is**.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Subjects Joined by 'and' (Rules 1-3)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
What is the difference between "My uncle and my guardian are helping me" and "My uncle and guardian is helping me"?

**My uncle and my guardian are helping me** — the possessive *my* is repeated, so two persons are meant (plural verb).
**My uncle and guardian is helping me** — *my* is used once, so one person (my uncle, who is also my guardian) is meant (singular verb).

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Subjects Joined by 'and' (Rules 1-3)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
What is the difference between "The secretary and the cashier were arrested" and "The secretary and cashier was arrested"?

**The secretary and the cashier were arrested** — *the* is repeated: two persons, plural verb.
**The secretary and cashier was arrested** — *the* is used once: one person holding both posts, singular verb.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Collective Nouns (Rule 5)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
What is the difference between "Our team is playing today" and "The team are taking rest now"?

**Our team is playing today** — the team is thought of as **one unit**, so the verb is singular.
**The team are taking rest now** — the speaker is thinking of the **individual members** (each player resting), so the verb is plural. (This plural use is typical of British and Indian English.)

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Collective Nouns (Rule 5)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
What is the difference between "The clergy is not to blame" and "The clergy are against the new law"?

**The clergy is not to blame** — the clergy as a single body (singular).
**The clergy are against the new law** — the individual members of the clergy and their opinions (plural).

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Collective Nouns (Rule 5)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
What is the difference between "The Government welcomes the proposal" and "The Government are discussing the proposal"?

**The Government welcomes the proposal** — the Government acts as one unit, giving one decision (singular).
**The Government are discussing the proposal** — the members are discussing among themselves (plural).

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: one of, a lot of, many a, a good many (Rules 9-13)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
What is the difference between "Many a passenger was hurt" and "A good many passengers were hurt"?

Both mean that many passengers were hurt, but the grammar differs:
- **Many a** + singular noun + **singular verb**: *Many a passenger **was** hurt.*
- **A good many** + plural noun + **plural verb**: *A good many passengers **were** hurt.*

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: one of, a lot of, many a, a good many (Rules 9-13)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
Why do we say "Sheep are meek animals" but "A sheep was run over by a car"?

*Sheep* has the **same form in the singular and the plural**. In *A sheep was run over*, the article *a* shows that **one** sheep is meant, so the verb is singular. In *Sheep are meek animals*, sheep in general (plural) are meant, so the verb is plural.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Subjects Joined by 'and' (Rules 1-3)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
Correct the subject-verb agreement in this sentence: "Gopal and Ganesh is cousins."

**Gopal and Ganesh are cousins.**
A compound subject joined by *and* takes a plural verb.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: Subjects Joined by 'and' (Rules 1-3)

Correct the subject-verb agreement in this sentence: "Bread and butter were served for breakfast."

**Bread and butter was served for breakfast.**
*Bread and butter* stands for one idea (one dish), so the verb is singular.

With *as well as*, the verb agrees with the first noun, *The President* (singular).

Correct the subject-verb agreement in this sentence: "The police is vigilant."

A distance is treated as one quantity, so the verb is singular.

**An aircraft was damaged while taking off.**
*An* shows that one aircraft is meant, so the verb is singular.

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
Correct the subject-verb agreement in this sentence: "Many a passengers were hurt in the accident."

**Many a passenger was hurt in the accident.**
*Many a* takes a singular noun and a singular verb.

section: 12.2 Rules of Concord: one of, a lot of, many a, a good many (Rules 9-13)

messages.content: You are an expert English grammar tutor. Explain rules clearly and simply, give correct answers, and briefly justify each answer.
Correct the subject-verb agreement in this sentence: "A great deal of discussions have taken place on the matter."

**A great many discussions have taken place on the matter.**
*A great deal of* is used with uncountable nouns. With a plural countable noun, use *a great many* (plural verb). Alternatively: *A great deal of discussion has taken place on the matter.*
